cards.text: Ezekiel is a priest living among the exiles by the River Kebar (Ezekiel 1:1-3). God has just told him to shut himself inside his house (Ezekiel 3:24). Now the Lord gives him a job, and friend, it starts with... a brick. Not a scroll. Not a trumpet. A BRICK.

cards.question: God tells Ezekiel to set a brick in front of him and draw on it the city of ___.

cards.text: City drawn. Now God tells Ezekiel to lay siege against it. Friend, I once spent a whole afternoon laying siege to a stuck jar of sprinkles, and I LOST.

cards.question: God tells Ezekiel to build a ramp to the city on the brick and set up camps against it.

cards.text: Next, God says to take an iron plate and set it up as an iron wall between Ezekiel and the city. Then Ezekiel turns his face toward it and besieges it.

cards.question: God says Ezekiel's brick, siege and iron wall will be what for the house of Israel?

cards.text: Then comes the hard part. God tells Ezekiel to lie down on his left side and place the iniquity of the house of Israel upon himself.

cards.question: God assigns Ezekiel a number of days on his left side. Each day stands for one ___ of Israel's iniquity.

cards.text: God sets the count at 390 days. On his LEFT side. Friend, I can't stay on one side through a single snooze button.

cards.question: After his days on his left side for Israel, Ezekiel lies down on his right side. Whose iniquity does he bear there?
Ezekiel's time on his right side for Judah is longer than his 390 days on his left side for Israel.

cards.text: Through all of it, Ezekiel keeps his face turned toward the siege of Jerusalem, with his arm bared.

cards.question: With his face toward the siege of Jerusalem and his arm bared, what is Ezekiel to do?

cards.text: And God leaves zero wiggle room. He says, “Now behold, I will tie you up with ropes…”

cards.question: Before the days of his siege are finished, Ezekiel can roll over to his other side whenever he gets tired.

cards.text: Ezekiel has his days on his side. Now God gives him the menu: wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet and spelt, all made into bread for himself.

cards.question: God gives Ezekiel six ingredients for his bread. How does He tell him to put them together?

cards.text: One container. One bread. 390 days. Friend, that's not a recipe, that's my topping bins at closing time. And God has Ezekiel weigh out twenty shekels of it a day.

cards.question: Ezekiel weighs out his food each day, and he is to eat it at set ___.

cards.text: His water gets measured too: a sixth of a hin, drunk at set times. A SIXTH. Friend, a sixth of anything has never been a lot.
Then God tells Ezekiel how to bake it. He's to eat it like a barley cake, baked over dried human excrement, in the sight of the people.

cards.question: God says Ezekiel's bread shows how the Israelites will eat their defiled bread. Where will they eat it?

cards.text: And for the first time in this passage, Ezekiel speaks up. “Ah, Lord GOD,” he says. I bet his stomach just dropped to the floor.

cards.question: Ezekiel answers God's baking orders. What does he tell God about himself?

answers.text: He has never baked bread before
He is too weak to build a fire

cards.question: Ezekiel tells God he ate unclean meat only once, back in his youth.

cards.text: So Ezekiel lays it all out, honest and plain. Now, friend, watch how God answers him.

cards.question: God lets Ezekiel bake his bread over cow dung instead of human excrement.

cards.text: Then God tells Ezekiel what's coming: “Son of man, I am going to cut off the supply of food in Jerusalem.”

cards.question: Remember Ezekiel weighing his food and measuring his water? In Jerusalem, people will anxiously eat bread rationed by ___ and in despair drink water by ___.

cards.text: So they will lack food and water. No jokes on this one, friend. This is a heavy word.

cards.question: As Jerusalem lacks food and water, what will the people be appalled to see?

findings.problem: The opening card has six sentences: 'Ezekiel is a priest…', 'God has just told him…', 'Now the Lord gives him a job…', 'Not a scroll.', 'Not a trumpet.', 'A BRICK.' The limit is three.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'City drawn.', 'Now God tells Ezekiel…', 'Friend, I once spent…'.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: 'Then Ezekiel turns his face toward it and besieges it' tells this as something Ezekiel does. In Ezekiel 4:3 it is only God's command. The passage never says Ezekiel carried it out, and the text does not clearly imply it.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: 'God sets the count at 390 days.', 'On his LEFT side.', 'Friend, I can't stay…'.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer stands out. 'The house of Judah' echoes 'the house of Israel' from the cards before it, while both wrong answers use 'The land of…'. A baker can spot the right answer from its wording.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: No card tells the baker how many days Ezekiel lies on his right side. That makes this true-or-false a coin flip, not an informed guess.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The 40 days on Ezekiel's right side for Judah, 'a day for each year' (Ezekiel 4:6), is never stated on any card. The baker leaves without this key detail of the sign.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: 'Through all of it, Ezekiel keeps his face turned toward the siege of Jerusalem' tells God's command in Ezekiel 4:7 as something Ezekiel does. The passage only gives the command.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: 'That's not a recipe, that's my topping bins at closing time' pokes fun at the bread recipe God Himself gave Ezekiel (Ezekiel 4:9). The joke targets God's instruction, not Ezekiel's human situation.

rule.text: His humor never targets God, Jesus, Scripture or the Marriage Supper.
